description: How the UK's uncodified constitution distributes power across its key institutions.
content_html:
What Is a Constitution?

Every country needs a set of rules about how power is organised and who can do what. These rules form a constitution. In most countries, such as the United States, France and Germany, the constitution is a single written document. The UK is unusual because it does not have a single written constitution document. Instead, the UK has an uncodified constitution — its rules come from several different sources and have developed over centuries.

Sources of the British Constitution

The British constitution draws on several sources. The most important are: Acts of Parliament (such as the Human Rights Act 1998, the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, and the Devolution Acts of 1998); historical documents such as Magna Carta (1215) and the Bill of Rights (1689); court judgements that establish legal precedents; and constitutional conventions. Conventions are not enforceable in court but are considered politically binding — for example, the convention that the monarch invites the leader of the party with a parliamentary majority to form a government.

This mixture of written laws, historical documents and unwritten conventions means the British constitution is flexible and can be changed by Parliament passing a new Act. Supporters of the uncodified constitution argue this flexibility allows the constitution to adapt to changing circumstances without a lengthy amendment process. Critics argue it leaves too much power in the hands of the government and lacks the clear checks and balances found in codified constitutions. Both viewpoints reflect genuine ongoing debates about constitutional reform in the UK.

Key Fact

The British constitution is uncodified — it is not contained in one single document. Its sources include Acts of Parliament (e.g. Human Rights Act 1998), historical documents (e.g. Magna Carta 1215), court judgements and constitutional conventions. The constitution can be changed by Parliament passing new legislation.

The Key Institutions That Share Power

The British constitution distributes power among several key institutions. Understanding how each fits together is central to understanding how the UK is governed. The three main branches of government are the legislature, the executive, and the judiciary. The UK also has a constitutional monarchy.

The legislature is Parliament — the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Parliament makes law, scrutinises the government, controls taxation and debates public policy. The House of Commons is elected by the public; the House of Lords is mostly appointed. Parliament is said to be sovereign — meaning it has the supreme power to make and unmake any law.

The executive is the government: the Prime Minister, the Cabinet and government ministers. The Prime Minister leads the government and is appointed by the monarch, by convention, as the leader of the party with a majority in the House of Commons. The Cabinet is a committee of senior ministers who collectively decide policy. The civil service — permanent, politically neutral officials — carries out the day-to-day work of government departments, ministries and agencies.

The judiciary consists of the courts and judges. The UK’s highest court is the Supreme Court, established in 2009, which replaced the Law Lords. Courts interpret law and can declare that government action is unlawful, though courts cannot strike down Acts of Parliament the way constitutional courts can in some other countries. The judiciary’s independence from the government is a vital protection for citizens’ rights.

The monarchy plays a largely ceremonial role in the modern UK. The monarch formally opens Parliament, gives royal assent to Bills (formally approving them as law) and invites the Prime Minister to form a government. In practice, the monarch acts on the advice of the Prime Minister and ministers. The political power once held by the monarchy has transferred over centuries to Parliament and the elected government.

The British constitution is not fixed — it has changed significantly in recent decades. Devolution transferred significant powers to the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) and the Northern Ireland Assembly following Acts passed in 1998. These bodies have the power to legislate on devolved matters such as health and education in their regions, while Westminster retains reserved powers such as defence and foreign affairs.

The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law, giving courts the power to declare legislation incompatible with human rights — though only Parliament can change the legislation itself. The UK’s departure from the European Union in January 2020 also changed the constitutional landscape: EU law no longer has supremacy over UK law, and Parliament has reclaimed legislative competence in many areas. These ongoing changes illustrate the flexible, evolving nature of the uncodified constitution.

Key Fact

Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament is the supreme law-making authority in the UK. It can make, amend or repeal any law. No other body — not even the courts — can overrule an Act of Parliament. This is a central feature of the British constitution and is linked to the absence of a higher ‘constitutional’ law that Parliament cannot change.

It is a common misconception that the UK has no written constitution. Many parts of the UK constitution ARE written — for example, the Human Rights Act 1998, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, and Magna Carta are all written documents. What makes the UK constitution ‘uncodified’ is that these rules are not gathered together in a single supreme document as they are in the United States. Instead, the constitution is spread across multiple sources including Acts, conventions, and common law. The distinction to remember is: codified means gathered in one document; uncodified does not mean entirely unwritten.
exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark ‘Analyse’ question about the constitution, examiners look for two-sided analysis. A common mistake is describing features of the constitution without evaluating them — for example, stating that the constitution is flexible without then weighing whether flexibility is a strength or a weakness. Structure your answer: identify and explain the feature (e.g. uncodified constitution), then give an argument in its favour (flexibility, can adapt quickly), then give a counterargument (less clear protection of rights, government can alter it more easily). Name at least one real Act or example (Human Rights Act 1998, Devolution Acts 1998). For 12-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, a substantiated conclusion is essential — phrases like “overall, I think the uncodified constitution is a strength because…” earn marks that a simple summary does not.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UK has an uncodified constitution — its rules come from Acts of Parliament, historical documents, court judgements and conventions, not a single written document.
  • Power is shared between three branches: the legislature (Parliament), the executive (Prime Minister and Cabinet) and the judiciary (courts); the monarchy plays a largely ceremonial constitutional role.
  • Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament is supreme and can make or change any law; the constitution is flexible and has changed significantly through devolution, the Human Rights Act 1998 and the UK’s departure from the EU.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an uncodified constitution?
A) A constitution that bans any changes to the law
B) A constitution contained in one single written document
C) A constitution made up of several sources including Acts, conventions and court judgements
D) A constitution that gives all power to the monarch
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) A constitution made up of several sources including Acts, conventions and court judgements.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by parliamentary sovereignty.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. 1 mark for a basic correct statement (e.g. Parliament is the supreme law-making authority). 1 mark for development or precision (e.g. Parliament can make, change or repeal any law and no other body can overrule an Act of Parliament). A single-word or vague answer such as 'Parliament has power' scores 0-1 only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the British constitution.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks; 2 marks per feature. For each feature: 1 mark for identifying it, 1 mark for developing it with specific detail. Example features: (1) Uncodified — not contained in one single document, drawn from multiple sources including Acts of Parliament, conventions and court judgements. (2) Parliamentary sovereignty — Parliament is the supreme law-making authority and can make or change any law. (3) Flexible — can be changed by Parliament passing new legislation without a lengthy amendment process. (4) Constitutional conventions — unwritten but accepted practices such as the monarch acting on the advice of the Prime Minister. Evaluation or argument for/against is not required and not credited in a Describe question.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

"A leading constitutional reform campaign group published a report in 2024 arguing that the UK's uncodified constitution gives governments too much power with too few checks. The report stated: 'In the absence of a single written constitutional document, it is too easy for a government with a large majority to pass laws that significantly alter the relationship between the state and the citizen without any higher-law protection in place.'"

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does the source suggest about a possible weakness of the UK's constitution?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying a specific claim in the source (e.g. the argument that the uncodified constitution allows governments with large majorities to pass laws too easily). 1 mark for interpreting what this means (e.g. there is no entrenched higher law that Parliament cannot override, unlike in codified systems). 1 mark for applying own knowledge (e.g. comparing with the US constitution where amendments require two-thirds majorities; or noting that the Human Rights Act, while important, can itself be amended or repealed by Parliament). 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. weighing whether this is a significant weakness or whether parliamentary scrutiny and conventions provide sufficient checks). Pure summary of the source without interpretation caps at 1-2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Analyse whether the uncodified British constitution provides sufficient protection for citizens' rights.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Presents a well-developed, two-sided analysis with a substantiated judgement. Includes named real-world examples (e.g. Human Rights Act 1998 as protection; ability to repeal the HRA as a limitation; role of Supreme Court in reviewing executive action). Uses accurate constitutional vocabulary (parliamentary sovereignty, uncodified, conventions). Reaches a clear, substantiated overall judgement about whether protection is sufficient.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides present, at least one named example, generally accurate, some development of argument.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant content but one-sided, or both sides mentioned but underdeveloped. Limited real-world reference.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about rights or constitution. Little or no example. Descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text:
'The uncodified British constitution is a strength, not a weakness, for UK democracy.'

Evaluate this statement. In your answer consider arguments for and against and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): A sustained two-sided evaluation with multiple named real-world examples per side (e.g. flexibility and adaptability through the Devolution Acts 1998 and Human Rights Act 1998 as strengths; risks of government overreach, lack of entrenched rights, and role of unelected Lords as weaknesses). Reaches a clear substantiated judgement with reasoning. Deploys accurate vocabulary throughout (sovereignty, uncodified, conventions, legislature, executive, judiciary).

Secure (7-9 marks): Both viewpoints addressed, at least one named example, a judgement reached though possibly less nuanced.

Developing (4-6 marks): Some two-sided content but limited development or vague examples. Judgement may be weak.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic description of features. Little or no real-world reference. No meaningful overall judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What does it mean to say the UK has an 'uncodified' constitution?
options: The constitution is not contained in a single document but comes from several sources
The constitution cannot be changed by Parliament
The constitution is only made up of court judgements

knowledge_checks.q: Which branch of government is responsible for interpreting and applying the law through the courts?
The _____ means Parliament is the supreme law-making authority in the UK and can make, amend or repeal any law.
_____ are unwritten but accepted practices that govern how public institutions behave, such as the monarch acting on the Prime Minister's advice.
Match each institution to its role in the British constitution:
right: Runs the country (Prime Minister and Cabinet)

flashcard_questions.a: The fundamental rules determining how a country is governed and how power is distributed.
Its rules come from multiple sources, not one single written document.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three sources of the British constitution.
flashcard_questions.a: Acts of Parliament, constitutional conventions, court judgements.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Magna Carta and when was it signed?
flashcard_questions.a: A 1215 document limiting royal power; an early source of constitutional law.
Parliament is the supreme law-making authority; no body can overrule an Act of Parliament.
An unwritten but accepted practice governing how public institutions behave.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the executive in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: To put laws into practice and run the country — led by the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the legislature?
flashcard_questions.a: To make laws — in the UK this is Parliament (Commons and Lords).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of the judiciary?
flashcard_questions.a: To interpret and apply the law through the courts, independent of government.

flashcard_questions.q: What ceremonial role does the monarch play when a Bill is passed?
flashcard_questions.a: The monarch gives royal assent, formally approving the Bill as law.

flashcard_questions.q: Which 1998 Act transferred powers to the Scottish Parliament, Senedd and Northern Ireland Assembly?

flashcard_questions.a: The transfer of powers from Westminster to regional assemblies or parliaments.

glossary_terms.definition: The set of fundamental rules, laws and principles that determine how a country is governed, how power is distributed and what rights citizens hold.
A constitution that is not contained in a single written document but is made up of Acts of Parliament, court judgements, conventions and other sources.
Unwritten but accepted practices and traditions that govern how public institutions behave, such as the monarch acting on the advice of the Prime Minister.
The branch of government responsible for making laws; in the UK this is Parliament (House of Commons and House of Lords).
The branch of government responsible for putting laws into practice and running the country, led by the Prime Minister and cabinet.
The branch of government responsible for interpreting and applying the law through the courts, independent of Parliament and the government.
The transfer of legislative and executive powers from Westminster Parliament to regional assemblies or parliaments in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
